summary:
I've been spending most of my time lately on infrastructure that has to share one piece of hardware honestly, plus grounding an AI assistant so it stops making things up.

The GPU problem: I run a single 16GB card and half a dozen different models want it — a chat brain, an image generator, a roleplay model, a smaller summarizer. Only one big model fits at a time, so I built Switchboard, a small proxy that serializes access — it evicts whoever's holding the card, waits for VRAM to actually drop, then loads the next one. The interesting bit came later: I wired a vision adapter onto the production brain and it turned out to be free — same 262K context, no drop in decode speed, just a few hundred extra megabytes of memory. The card can now read screenshots without anything else changing. (I also learned the hard way that a container's restart policy doesn't save you from an explicit stop — one setting difference cost the whole thing an hour of downtime after a reboot, silently, with nothing paging me about it.)

On a client project — a tabletop-gaming companion app — a live session had everyone joined on video but nobody could hear anyone. Took a while to track down: the video library was correctly receiving everyone's audio track, it just never attached it to an actual audio element, so the sound arrived and had nowhere to go. Fixed that, plus a related bug where players without a working webcam couldn't join a call at all, since one failed device check was blocking the whole handshake.

The AI assistant on that same app had a worse problem: asked about a specific character ability, it confidently invented an answer instead of saying it didn't know. I traced it to four separate causes stacked on top of each other — the prompt claimed access to books it didn't actually have, the fallback behavior explicitly permitted guessing when nothing was found, temperature was too high for a factual lookup, and (the one that surprised me) the character import pipeline was silently dropping subclass features, so the AI wasn't even lying about content it had — it genuinely didn't have it. Fixed all four and it now says "I don't have that" and asks which book it's from. Chasing that bug also turned up a separate privacy issue: re-indexing a document was dropping a visibility tag, which meant editing a supposedly private, GM-only note could quietly make it readable by the whole group. Worth having caught before anyone noticed the hard way.

On the more mundane side, I built a small set of read-only tools that let an AI agent query my personal budgeting app directly — account balances, spending by category — instead of me copy-pasting numbers into a chat. Not glamorous, but it's the kind of connective tissue that makes the rest of the automation actually useful day to day.

highlights.oneLiner: Serializes one GPU across chat/image/RP models; vision on the brain now free.
Added read-only MCP tools so an agent can query balances/spending directly.
